output:
Sound is a wave. Air pressure rises and falls, your eardrum moves in step, and your brain reads that movement as noise. The pressure pattern is the whole story.

Now consider what happens when two waves meet. If a rise arrives exactly alongside another rise, the sound grows louder. If a rise arrives alongside a fall of equal size, they cancel. The air simply stays still, and you hear nothing. Physicists call this destructive interference.

Noise-cancelling headphones exploit that cancellation deliberately. A tiny microphone on the outside of each earcup listens to the world around you. A small processor inside analyses that incoming wave and calculates its exact opposite: a mirror image where every peak becomes a trough. The headphone speaker then plays that opposite into your ear alongside the real sound. The two patterns meet and flatten each other out.

Picture a wave rolling up a beach while an identical wave rolls back down. Where they collide, the water goes briefly flat.

All of this happens in well under a thousandth of a second, which is why it must be done electronically rather than by any mechanical trick.

The method has limits. It handles steady, low rumbles well — aircraft engines, train carriages, air conditioning. Sudden, high-pitched sounds change too quickly for the processor to mirror in time, so voices and clattering cutlery often still get through. Padding around your ears blocks some of those by brute force instead.

In short, the headphones listen to the noise and play its exact opposite, so the two cancel before reaching your eardrum.
